title: Sharps, waste, linen, spillages and decontamination
blurb: Handle sharps safely, respond to a sharps injury, choose the right waste stream and deal with spills, linen and equipment.
question: While giving a subcutaneous injection to a patient with hepatitis C, a nurse sustains a needlestick injury through her glove. What should she do first?

teach.body: Four of the ten standard precautions deal with what is left after care: sharps and occupational exposure, waste, linen, and spills and equipment. They protect staff, porters, cleaners, laundry workers and the next patient. The Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 set the legal duties for sharps, HTM 07-01 governs healthcare waste, and the NIPCM sets the day-to-day practice for nurses in England.

items: Avoid unnecessary use of sharps; where a sharp is needed, use a safer sharp device and activate its safety mechanism.
Do not resheath (recap) or disassemble needles.
Do not pass sharps directly from hand to hand.
The person who used the sharp discards it at the point of use, needle and syringe as one unit.
Sharps containers: handle, temporary closure when not in use, labelled with origin and dates, closed and replaced at the fill line.
Report all sharps injuries and near misses to your line manager or employer.

Bags no more than two-thirds full, closed with a swan neck or plastic tie, traceable to the ward, stored in a locked area.

values: Any used linen, soiled or not
Used by a patient known or suspected to be infectious

values: Used linen hamper, no more than two-thirds full
Water-soluble (alginate) bag, then an impermeable outer bag

values: Remove one item at a time
Roll up, do not sort, seal before leaving the area

teach.caption: Never shake, rinse or sort used linen, never put it on the floor or a locker, and do not re-handle it once bagged.

teach.caption: Finish every spill with detergent and warm water, dry the area, discard PPE and towels as healthcare waste, then hand hygiene.

teach.body: Equipment marked with a 2 in a circle with a line through it is single use: used once on one patient and discarded. Single patient use items, such as a nebuliser mask, may be reused on the same person. Needles and syringes are single use: never reuse them to draw up more medication, and never give medication from a single-dose vial or IV bag to more than one patient. Check sterile packs are intact, in date and uncontaminated before use.

Hana is giving subcutaneous heparin to Mr Peters, 61, who has hepatitis C, when the needle goes through her glove into her finger. She lets the wound bleed without squeezing, washes it under warm running water with soap, and does not suck or scrub it. She covers it, tells the nurse in charge straight away, completes an incident report and goes to occupational health (or A&E out of hours) for a risk assessment. She makes sure the needle has been disposed of safely.

teach.text: Two chlorine strengths, two jobs: 10,000 ppm (or granules) for BLOOD and high-risk body fluids; 1,000 ppm for urine, faeces, vomit, isolation rooms and C. difficile cleaning. And never pour chlorine straight onto urine.

items: No recapping, no hand-to-hand passing; the user discards sharps at the point of use; replace containers at the fill line.
Exposure: bleed, wash with soap and warm running water, no squeezing or sucking, report, occupational health.
Orange = infectious; tiger = offensive; yellow = medicines; purple = cytotoxic; blue = medicines without sharps; red lid = anatomical.
Infectious linen: alginate bag inside an impermeable bag; never shake or sort.
Blood spills: granules or 10,000 ppm. Other body fluids: 1,000 ppm; no chlorine directly on urine.

summary: You can now apply the Sharps Regulations, give first aid and report after an exposure, choose the correct waste stream and manage infectious linen. You can also choose the right chlorine strength for blood, other body fluids and equipment.

A.q: Nurse Hana sustains a needlestick injury through her glove while injecting a patient with hepatitis C. What should she do first?
options: Squeeze the wound hard to empty it, then apply an alcohol swab to the site
Let it bleed without squeezing and wash with soap and running water
Suck the wound, then cover it with a waterproof plaster
Scrub the area with a nail brush and chlorhexidine soap for two minutes
A.why: NIPCM appendix 10: allow the area to bleed without squeezing, do not suck it, and wash with warm running water and soap, then report the incident.

whyNot.0: Squeezing is advised against and alcohol is not the first aid recommended.
whyNot.2: Sucking the wound is specifically advised against.
whyNot.3: Scrubbing damages tissue and can increase uptake of the virus.

A.q: Pauline has an MRSA-colonised leg ulcer. The nurse removes a dressing heavily soaked with exudate. In an acute hospital, which waste stream is correct?
options: Yellow and black tiger-striped offensive waste bag
Black domestic waste bag
Purple cytotoxic waste bag
Orange infectious clinical waste bag
A.why: Waste from a patient known or suspected to be infected or colonised is infectious clinical waste: orange bag (NIPCM table 1).

whyNot.0: Offensive waste is non-infectious; this dressing is from a colonised wound.
whyNot.1: Domestic waste is not a route for a dressing from an MRSA-colonised wound, which is infectious clinical waste.
whyNot.2: Purple is for waste contaminated with cytotoxic or cytostatic medicines.

A.q: During a medicines round, Lewis notices the sharps container on the trolley has reached the manufacturer's fill line. What should he do?
options: Press the contents down to make room for more
Close and lock it, label it with origin and date, and replace it
Transfer some of the contents into a second, empty sharps container
Keep using it carefully until the end of the medicines round
A.why: Sharps containers are disposed of when the fill line is reached and are labelled with point of origin and dates (NIPCM 1.9).

whyNot.0: Pressing down contents risks a sharps injury.
whyNot.2: Transferring used sharps between containers is unsafe handling.
whyNot.3: Overfilling beyond the fill line increases injury risk.

B.q: Blood from a dislodged cannula has spilled onto the hard floor beside Thomas's bed. Spill granules are available. The nurse has put on gloves and an apron. What next?
options: Soak it up with paper towels, then clean with 1,000 ppm chlorine solution
Cover it with towels and call the domestic team
Wipe it up with detergent and warm water
Apply chlorine-releasing granules and leave for the contact time
B.why: For blood, chlorine-releasing granules are applied directly (or 10,000 ppm solution on towels), left for the contact time (about 3 minutes), then cleaned with detergent (NIPCM appendix 9).

whyNot.0: 1,000 ppm is the strength for urine, faeces or vomit, not blood.
whyNot.1: Spills are treated immediately by trained staff; leaving one covered delays decontamination.
whyNot.2: Detergent alone does not disinfect a blood spill.

B.q: A urinal containing no visible blood is knocked over in a bay. The nurse is wearing gloves and an apron. What is the correct method?
options: Pour 10,000 ppm chlorine solution over the spill and leave for 3 minutes
Sprinkle chlorine-releasing granules onto the urine
Soak up with paper towels, then clean with 1,000 ppm chlorine
Mop with the ward's general mop and hot water
B.why: Urine is soaked up first with paper towels (a gelling agent may be used), then the area is cleaned with 1,000 ppm available chlorine. Chlorine must not be applied directly to urine (NIPCM appendix 9).

whyNot.0: Chlorine must not be applied directly to urine, and 10,000 ppm is for blood.
whyNot.1: Granules are chlorine-releasing and must not go directly onto urine.
whyNot.3: A shared mop spreads contamination and plain hot water does not disinfect.

B.q: Ivy, 85, has confirmed norovirus and her bed linen is soiled with diarrhoea. How should the linen be bagged?
options: Shake it into the used linen hamper
Rinse it in the sluice, then bag it as used linen
Roll it up and seal it in a water-soluble bag inside an impermeable bag
Sort it at the bedside, then bag the most heavily soiled items separately
B.why: Infectious linen is not sorted but rolled together and sealed in a water-soluble (alginate) bag, then placed in an impermeable bag before leaving the area (NIPCM 1.7).

whyNot.0: Shaking linen disperses organisms, and this is infectious, not used, linen.
whyNot.1: Linen must not be rinsed on removal.
whyNot.3: Infectious linen must not be sorted.

C.q: You see a colleague give an IM injection to Lily, then carefully recap the needle with both hands to carry it to the sharps container at the nurses' station. What should you advise?
options: Take a sharps container to the point of use and do not recap
Use the one-handed scoop technique whenever she needs to recap
Carry the uncapped needle to the container very carefully
Pass the needle to a colleague who is nearer the container
C.why: Under the Sharps Regulations and NIPCM, needles are not recapped, and sharps are discarded at the point of use by the person who used them, so the container is taken to the patient.

whyNot.1: Recapping by any technique is not the standard; disposal at the point of use removes the need.
whyNot.2: Walking with an exposed used needle risks injury; the container comes to the bedside.
whyNot.3: Sharps must not be passed directly hand to hand.

C.q: A communal commode has been used by Frank, who has suspected C. difficile. It must be decontaminated before anyone else uses it. Which method is correct?
options: Wipe with detergent and leave to dry
Wipe all of its surfaces with alcohol wipes and leave it to air dry
Clean with detergent, then 1,000 ppm chlorine, rinse and dry
Spray with 10,000 ppm chlorine and leave it wet
C.why: Equipment used by a patient with infection is cleaned with detergent followed by 1,000 ppm available chlorine (or a combined product), following contact time and drying (NIPCM appendix 7).

whyNot.0: Detergent alone is for routine decontamination, not after an infected patient.
whyNot.1: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores.
whyNot.3: 10,000 ppm is for blood contamination, and equipment must be dried before storage.

C.q: A nurse draws up an injection for one patient and finds some drug left in the single-dose vial. A second patient on the same ward is prescribed the same drug and dose. What should she do?
options: Use a new syringe and needle to draw from the same vial for the second patient
Use the same syringe with a fresh needle for the second patient
Label the vial with the time and use it within 24 hours
Discard the remaining drug and use a new vial for the second patient
C.why: The NIPCM states medications from a single-dose vial must never be given to more than one patient, and needles and syringes are single use.

whyNot.0: A new syringe does not make a single-dose vial safe to share between patients.
whyNot.1: Syringes must never be reused, even with a new needle.
whyNot.2: Labelling and time limits apply to some multi-dose vials, not single-dose vials.

reteach.title: Think of who handles it next
reteach.question: Once you finish, who will touch this needle, bag, sheet or floor after you?

blocks.body: Porters carry waste bags, laundry staff open linen bags, cleaners mop floors and the next patient sits on the commode. Each rule exists to protect one of them: no overfilled bags (porters), alginate bags so infectious linen goes into the washer unopened (laundry), the right chlorine for the right spill (cleaners and patients), and sharps in a container at the bedside (everyone).

blocks.text: Orange = infectious. Yellow-and-black tiger = offensive, NOT infectious. Purple = cytotoxic.

explain.body: Avoid unnecessary sharps; use safer sharps; no recapping; dispose at the point of use; employers must provide information and training, and arrange response, investigation and records after injuries.

test.q: Under the Sharps Regulations 2013, what is the first approach to reducing sharps injuries?
options: Wearing double gloves for injections
Placing sharps bins at the nurses' station
Recapping needles with one hand
Avoiding unnecessary use of sharps
test.why: The basic guidance is to avoid unnecessary use of sharps; if a sharp cannot be avoided, use a safer sharp device.

whyNot.0: Double gloving is not recommended for routine care and is not the primary control.
whyNot.1: Containers belong at the point of use, not a central station.

explain.body: Let it bleed, do not squeeze or suck, wash with warm running water and soap; irrigate eyes or mouth with water; report and attend occupational health or A&E as required.

test.q: Blood splashes into a nurse's eye while she removes an arterial line. What is the first step?
options: Irrigate the eye copiously with water
Rub the eye to remove the blood
Apply an antiseptic eye drop to the affected eye
Cover the eye and finish the task
test.why: For eye or mouth exposure, rinse or irrigate copiously with water (removing contact lenses and irrigating again), then report (NIPCM appendix 10).

whyNot.1: Rubbing can spread the blood and damage the eye surface.
whyNot.2: Antiseptic drops are not the first aid recommended.
whyNot.3: First aid is immediate; delaying increases exposure.

explain.body: Orange infectious; tiger offensive; yellow medicines or chemicals; purple cytotoxic; blue medicines without sharps; red-lidded anatomical and full blood bags; black or clear domestic. Two-thirds full, swan neck, traceable.

test.q: An incontinence pad from a patient with no known or suspected infection is removed in hospital. Which waste stream is appropriate?
options: Orange infectious clinical waste bag
Purple cytotoxic waste
Yellow and black offensive waste
Blue pharmaceutical waste
test.why: Non-infectious waste containing body fluids, secretions or excretions is offensive waste: the yellow and black tiger bag.

whyNot.0: Orange is for waste from patients known or suspected to be infectious.
whyNot.1: Purple is for cytotoxic or cytostatic contamination.

explain.body: Infectious linen: alginate bag then impermeable bag. Shared equipment: detergent between patients; detergent then 1,000 ppm after an infected patient; 10,000 ppm for blood.

test.q: What makes an alginate bag suitable for infectious linen?
options: It dissolves in the wash so staff do not handle the linen
It is strong enough to hold heavy wet linen without leaking
It contains a disinfectant that treats the linen
It is coloured to warn staff of a sharps risk
test.why: Alginate (water-soluble) bags dissolve in the washing machine so laundry staff do not handle infectious linen; the outer impermeable bag contains leaks.

whyNot.1: Containment against leaks is the job of the outer impermeable bag.
whyNot.2: The bag does not contain a disinfectant.
whyNot.3: Linen bags must not contain sharps at all; colour is not a sharps warning.
